cells.tense: Right now the ending and the beginning are the same threshold, and you're standing at it awake.
cells.ask: Write down what this cycle taught you, one page, then put it where you'll find it again and stop working on it.
cells.core:
You know how to let a thing finish without slamming anything shut. When something reaches its end, you mark it — you say it's done — and you stay open to whatever comes next. That isn't indecision. It's the harder move: closing clearly while keeping the hinges loose.

The way it works for you is that each moment arrives as itself, fresh, and you meet it as it lands. Nothing gathers dust. So when you finish something, it's actually finished, and the next thing gets a clear surface to land on. The cost is attention. If you stop tracking what's arriving, this turns into drifting — things end without being marked and sit there taking up room you meant to clear.
cells.sheetLine: You close things cleanly and stay open to what comes next.
cells.verb: letting a thing finish so the next one can start
cells.place: at the threshold where something ends and whatever comes next crosses in

cells.tense: You'll have already declared this finished before it has actually run its course.
cells.ask: Pick the one thing you're most eager to call done and give it one more week, doing only what it still asks for.
cells.core:
Somewhere ahead is the moment this is over and signed off, and you're living there already. So you keep reaching for the ending — announcing it, packing it up, moving on — while the thing itself is still mid-course. The arrival you keep claiming hasn't happened yet.

What that costs is the part you skipped. You get the clean folder and the sense of a shut door; you don't get the loose thread finished or the lesson absorbed. And an ending you rushed toward doesn't hold, so it has to be done again. Notice what it feels like to let a thing run one beat past your urge to close it. That's where the timing lives, not in how ready you are to be done.
cells.sheetLine: You keep calling it finished before it has finished.

cells.tense: You walked through a door once, and you're still standing on the other side of it.
cells.ask: Choose one open thing and say out loud what finishing it would look like, then take the smallest step toward that today.
cells.core:
Nothing quite closes for you. Things wind down but you keep them open — a little loose, a little unfinished, still possible — and from the outside it looks like searching. From the inside it feels like not being sure, so you don't commit to an ending and you don't move on either. The cycles keep circling instead of completing.

What's starved here is your sense of this moment as new. You're still looking back at an earlier threshold, treating it as the live one, so nothing arriving now gets your full weight. Don't try to feel your way into closing — that isn't where it comes from. Do one small concrete act of finishing, even something tiny, and let the doing teach you what completion is like before you decide you're ready for it.

cells.tense: You've been writing this whole time, and the pen in your hand reads as though it isn't yours.
cells.ask: Name the one ending you're treating as still in motion and hand it over — tell someone it's done, and mean it.
cells.core:
Some cycles you're in are already closed and some aren't, and the difference isn't visible to you. You talk about your situation as though it were still unfolding, still undecided, still waiting — while part of it has quietly finished and part of it barely got going. The endings are real. What's missing is that you've marked them.

When release is available and you don't take it, the closed thing keeps its grip on your attention. Letting go of a finished cycle isn't a loss; it's clearing the table for what's actually in front of you. Start by telling one person, plainly, that something is over. The saying is what makes it yours — not the feeling, not a ceremony, just the sentence, out loud, to someone who can hear it.
cells.sheetLine: Some things have ended. You haven't said so yet.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim I'm closest to making is that the person has actually finished something and is refusing to see it — the record supports only that cycles close or don't, not that any particular cycle is done. A reader could reasonably say no, nothing has ended here, I have no sense of a door behind me. The ask survives being wrong because handing a plain inventory of what's finished, in their own view, is useful whether or not my read is right. The sentence that serves me more than them is any version of 'you already know it's over' — flattering and unfalsifiable; I've kept it out.
